title: मध्यकालमा बुद्ध धर्म Madhyakalma Buddha Dharma
authors: रञ्जितकार Ranjitkar, जुनु Junu बासुकला Basukala
nepali: मध्यकालमा बुद्ध धर्म डा. जुनु बासुकला रञ्जितकार सारांश सन् ८७९ देखि १२०० सम्मको काललाई राजनैनिक रुपले अन्धकार युग भनिए पनि बौद्ध धर्मकोबज्रयानको दृष्टिकोणले हेर्दा चरम अवस्थामा पुगेको समय हो । त्यस समय बौद्ध धर्म, दर्शन, संस्कृत भाषाको अध्ययन अध्यायपनको लगि नेपाल, भारत र तिब्बतको अन्तराष्ट्रिय समन्वय हुँदा नेपाल पुलको रुपमा थियो ।यही समयमा संस्कृत बौद्ध साहित्यहरू प्रज्ञापारमिता, सद्धर्मपुण्डरीकसूत्र, पञ्चरक्षा, नामसंगीति आदि सारेर ग्रन्थ तयार गरी ग्रन्थमा चित्र पनि लेख्ने विकास भएको थियो । बाह्रौँ शताब्दीको अन्त्यतिर भारतमा बौद्ध धर्मको नाशहुनु र यहाँ मल्ल राजाको शासनको शुरू भएपछि काठमाडौँ उपत्यका बज्रयान बौद्ध धर्मको केन्द्र हुनुका साथै तान्त्रिक देवीदेवता पनि केन्द्रस्थल हुन पुग्यो । यहाँका राजाहरूले पनि विहार निर्माण, बौद्ध मूर्ति स्थापना, बौद्धजात्रा गर्नुका साथै तिनीहरू लामो समयसम्म संरक्षण र सम्वद्र्धनको लागि जग्गा जमीनहरू समेत राखे । यहीसमयमा नै ब्राह्मण धर्मको प्रवेश भएपछि खुशीले वा करबलले भिक्षु भिक्षुणीहरू गृहस्थी जीवनमा आउनुका साथै ब्राह्मण धर्ममा जस्तै बौद्धहरूमा पनि काम अनुसारको जात विभाजन कार्य पनि भयो । यही समयमा पश्चिम नेपालमा चारसय वर्षसम्म खस मल्ल राजाहरू बौद्ध धर्मका अनुयायी भएकाले बौद्ध धर्मको विकास हुनुका साथैविहार, चैत्य र बुद्धका मूर्तिहरू समेत स्थापना भएको थियो । मल्लकालको उत्तराद्र्धमा पुराना विहार र चैत्यहरूजीर्णोद्धार गर्नुका साथै नयाँ विहार र चैत्य निर्माणमा निरन्तरता नै भइरह्यो ।
american_english:
Buddhism in the Medieval Period — Dr. Junu Basukala Ranjitkar — Abstract
Although the period from 879 to 1200 CE was called the Dark Age in political terms, viewed from the standpoint of Vajrayana Buddhism it was a time that reached its extreme peak. At that time, when there was international coordination among Nepal, India and Tibet for the study and learning of Buddhism, philosophy and the Sanskrit language, Nepal was a bridge. In this same period, Sanskrit Buddhist texts such as the Prajnaparamita, Saddharmapundarika Sutra, Pancharaksha and Namasangiti were gathered into books, and the practice of illustrating them developed as well. Toward the end of the twelfth century, after Buddhism was destroyed in India and the Malla king's rule began here, the Kathmandu Valley became the center of Vajrayana Buddhism, and the tantric deities likewise came to be at the center. The kings here too, along with building viharas, installing Buddhist images and holding Buddhist festivals, also kept lands for the long-term protection and promotion of them. At this very time, after Brahmanism entered, monks and nuns came into householder life willingly or by force, and as in Brahmanism, caste division according to occupation also took place among the Buddhists. During this same period, the Khas Malla kings of western Nepal were followers of Buddhism for four hundred years, and along with the development of Buddhism, viharas, chaityas and images of the Buddha were also established. In the latter part of the Malla period, the old viharas and chaityas were renovated, and the construction of new viharas and chaityas continued without interruption.

During that era, when there was international collaboration among Nepal, India and Tibet for the study and pursuit of Buddhism, philosophy and the Sanskrit language, Nepal stood as a bridge. In that same era, Sanskrit Buddhist works such as the Prajnaparamita, Saddharmapundarika Sutra, Pancharaksha and Namasangiti were compiled into volumes, and the practice of illustrating them developed as well. Towards the end of the twelfth century, once Buddhism had perished in India and the rule of the Malla kings had begun here, the Kathmandu Valley became the centre of Vajrayana Buddhism, and the tantric deities likewise came to occupy the centre. The kings here also, besides building viharas, erecting Buddhist images and conducting Buddhist festivals, retained lands for their long-term protection and promotion. At this very time, after Brahmanism had entered, monks and nuns came into householder life, whether willingly or by force, and just as in Brahmanism, caste division according to occupation was carried out among the Buddhists too. informal_english:
Buddhism in the Middle Ages — Dr Junu Basukala Ranjitkar — Summary
Look, the stretch from 879 to 1200 gets called the Dark Ages in political circles, but through a Vajrayana Buddhist lens it was actually when things hit their peak. Back then, while Nepal, India and Tibet were co-ordinating internationally over the study of Buddhism, philosophy and Sanskrit, Nepal was the bridge in the middle. That same stretch saw Sanskrit Buddhist texts — Prajnaparamita, Saddharmapundarika Sutra, Pancharaksha, Namasangiti and so on — pulled together into books, and pretty soon they were being illustrated too. By the tail end of the twelfth century, once Buddhism had been wiped out in India and the Malla kings took over here, the Kathmandu Valley became the centre of Vajrayana Buddhism, and the tantric deities ended up smack in the middle of it all. The local kings got in on it too — they put up viharas, installed Buddha statues, ran Buddha festivals, and even handed over land to keep it all protected and promoted over the long haul. Around this same time Brahmanism came in, and monks and nuns started living the household life, whether they wanted to or were strong-armed into it, and — same as under Brahmanism — the Buddhists ended up with caste divisions based on occupation as well. That same period, the Khas Malla kings out west stuck with Buddhism for a solid four hundred years, and as it spread, viharas, chaityas and Buddha statues went up too. In the late Malla period, they were fixing up the old viharas and chaityas and putting up new ones, and they just kept at it.
